prompt: Scan the default top-1000 TCP ports of 10.0.0.5
why: Bare nmap = top 1000 TCP ports.

prompt: Scan ALL 65535 TCP ports of 10.0.0.5
why: -p- means every TCP port.

prompt: Detect service versions on 10.0.0.5
why: -sV fingerprints the software/version behind each port.

prompt: Fast SYN (half-open) scan of the 10.0.0.0/24 subnet
why: -sS never finishes the handshake: faster, quieter.

prompt: List listening TCP/UDP sockets with the owning program
why: t=tcp u=udp l=listening p=process n=numeric.

prompt: Show what the current user may run via sudo
why: First thing to check for Linux privesc.

prompt: Find SUID binaries anywhere on the filesystem
why: SUID binaries run as their owner - a privesc hunt.

prompt: List all running processes (full detail)
why: Classic full process listing.

prompt: List every computer in the domain
why: Enumerates all domain-joined machines.

prompt: List all domain controllers
why: DCs are the crown jewels of AD.

prompt: Show the members of Domain Admins
why: Who holds the keys to the domain.

prompt: List members of the local Administrators group
why: Who is admin on THIS box.

prompt: Show listening TCP connections (PowerShell)
why: PowerShell's answer to 'what's exposed here'.

prompt: Show your token's privileges (cmd/PowerShell)
why: SeImpersonate/SeBackup/SeDebug here are privesc gold.

prompt: Find failed-logon events in the Security log
why: Event 4625 = failed logon: spot brute force.

prompt: Crack raw-MD5 hashes in hashes.txt with John and rockyou.txt
why: Tell John the hash format and give it a wordlist.

prompt: Crack MD5 hashes in hashes.txt with hashcat and rockyou.txt
why: -m 0 = MD5, -a 0 = straight wordlist attack.

prompt: Show the passwords John has already cracked for hashes.txt
why: Reads cracked results from the pot file.

prompt: Fetch only the response headers of http://10.0.0.5
why: -I = HEAD request: headers only.

prompt: Make a verbose request to http://10.0.0.5 (show the exchange)
why: -v shows the full request/response, TLS and all.

prompt: Look up the MX (mail) records for example.com
why: MX = which server receives the domain's mail.

prompt: Test the id param of http://10.0.0.5/item?id=1 for SQLi, no prompts
why: --batch takes defaults so it runs unattended.

prompt: Show the 50 newest events in the System log
why: -MaxEvents caps the count, and Get-WinEvent returns the newest first. -Newest belongs to the older Get-EventLog.

prompt: List successful logons (event 4624) from the Security log
why: 4624 is a logon that worked; 4625 is one that failed. The hashtable filters at the source, which is far faster than filtering afterwards.

prompt: Find failed logons (event 4625) from the last 24 hours
why: StartTime is the oldest event you want. EndTime with the same value would return everything BEFORE yesterday.

prompt: Find user accounts that were created (event 4720)
why: 4720 = a user account was created. 4726 is the opposite: an account was deleted.

prompt: Find when the Security audit log was cleared (event 1102)
why: 1102 is written to the Security log itself when someone clears it. A cleared log is a finding.

prompt: Find services that were installed on this machine (event 7045)
why: 7045 lives in the System log (the Security log's version is 4697). A new service is a common way to stay on a machine.

prompt: Read PowerShell script-block logging events (event 4104)
why: 4104 records the script text that ran. It is in the Operational log, not the classic 'Windows PowerShell' log.

prompt: List every event log on this machine with its record count
why: -ListLog describes the logs; -LogName * would start reading every event in all of them.

prompt: Read the events in the saved log file C:\Cases\security.evtx
why: -Path reads an exported .evtx file, so you can work a case away from the machine. -LogName only names a live log.

prompt: List only the services that are running
why: Get-Service has no -Status parameter: filter its objects with Where-Object.

prompt: Show each service's start mode and the account it runs as
answer: Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Select-Object Name, StartMode, StartName
why: StartName is the account. It lives on the Win32_Service class, not on what Get-Service returns.

prompt: Show the program file behind the service named Spooler
why: PathName is the command the service starts. Check where it lives and who can write there.

prompt: Find services that are set to start automatically but are not running
why: An automatic service that is stopped either failed or was stopped by someone. Both are worth a look.

prompt: List the scheduled tasks that are not disabled
why: Ready and Running tasks will fire. Start an audit with the ones that can actually run.

prompt: Show what the scheduled task named Backup actually runs
why: Actions holds the program and its arguments. Get-ScheduledTaskInfo shows when it ran, not what.

prompt: Show when the scheduled task named Backup last ran, and with what result
why: LastRunTime and LastTaskResult are on the info object. Get-ScheduledTask alone shows only the state.

prompt: List the scheduled tasks that live outside the \Microsoft\ folder
why: Windows keeps its own tasks under \Microsoft\. What sits elsewhere was added by someone.

prompt: List the local accounts that are enabled
why: Enabled is a property to filter on. Get-LocalUser has no -Enabled parameter.

prompt: Show each local account's name, whether it is enabled, and its last logon
why: A local account calls it LastLogon. LastLogonDate is what Active Directory calls it.

prompt: Find the local accounts whose password never expires
why: A local account with no expiry has an empty PasswordExpires. PasswordNeverExpires is an Active Directory property.

prompt: List who may log on to this machine over Remote Desktop
why: Membership of Remote Desktop Users is what allows it. Remote Management Users is WinRM, a different door.

prompt: Show who has what access to C:\Shares\Finance
why: Access is the list of entries: who, allow or deny, and which rights. The Mode column of Get-ChildItem is attributes, not permissions.

prompt: Show the owner of C:\Shares\Finance
why: The owner can always change the permissions, so it matters. It is on the ACL, not on the item.

prompt: From the access list of C:\Shares\Finance, show only the entries for Everyone
why: IdentityReference names who the entry is for. An Everyone entry that allows writing is a finding.

prompt: Check whether C:\Shares\Finance has stopped inheriting permissions from its parent
why: True means inheritance is off and the folder carries its own list. IsInherited is a property of one entry, not of the folder.

prompt: Show whether the firewall is on for each profile
why: There are three profiles (Domain, Private, Public) and each has its own switch.

prompt: List the enabled inbound firewall rules that allow traffic
why: Without -Enabled True the list also holds rules that are switched off and let nothing in.
accept: get-netfirewallrule(?=.* -direction inbound)(?=.* -action allow)(?=.* -enabled true)( -(direction inbound|action allow|enabled true)){3}

prompt: List the outbound firewall rules that block traffic
why: Outbound block rules are what stops a program from calling out.

prompt: Show which ports the firewall rule with the display name 'Lab Web' covers
why: A rule object does not carry its ports. Pipe it to Get-NetFirewallPortFilter to see them.

prompt: Compute the SHA-256 hash of C:\Tools\agent.exe
why: SHA256 is the default, so no -Algorithm is needed. MD5 is not what a modern feed lists.

prompt: Compute the SHA-1 hash of C:\Tools\agent.exe (an old report lists SHA-1)
why: The algorithm names have no dash: SHA1, SHA256, SHA384, SHA512, MD5.

prompt: Hash every file under C:\Tools, subfolders included
why: Get-FileHash has no -Recurse. Let Get-ChildItem find the files and pipe them in.

prompt: Check the digital signature of C:\Tools\agent.exe
why: Status says Valid, NotSigned or HashMismatch, and SignerCertificate says who signed it.

prompt: List the running processes with the file each one runs from
why: A process object calls it Path. ExecutablePath is the Win32_Process name for the same thing.

prompt: Show the full command line of every running process
answer: Get-CimInstance Win32_Process | Select-Object ProcessId, Name, CommandLine
why: The command line is on Win32_Process. It shows the arguments a program was started with, which is where the story usually is.
wrong: Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Select-Object ProcessId, Name, CommandLine

prompt: Show every process with the process ID of its parent
answer: Get-CimInstance Win32_Process | Select-Object Name, ProcessId, ParentProcessId
why: The parent tells you what started it: a document viewer that starts a shell is a finding.

prompt: Show the process whose ID is 4242
why: A bare value is taken as a process NAME. An ID needs -Id.

prompt: Find which process owns the listener on TCP port 3389
why: A listener is a LOCAL port. OwningProcess is the ID to hand to Get-Process -Id.

prompt: List the UDP endpoints this machine is listening on
why: UDP has no connections, so it has its own cmdlet. Get-NetTCPConnection knows only TCP.

prompt: List the established TCP connections with their remote address, remote port and owning process
answer: Get-NetTCPConnection -State Established | Select-Object RemoteAddress, RemotePort, OwningProcess
why: Established means a live conversation. This is the answer to 'what is this machine talking to'.
wrong: Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen | Select-Object RemoteAddress, RemotePort, OwningProcess

prompt: List the disabled user accounts in the domain
why: Search-ADAccount has a switch for the common account audits. With Get-ADUser the filter is Enabled -eq $false: there is no Disabled attribute.

prompt: Find user accounts that have not logged on for 90 days
why: Inactive is about the last logon. -AccountExpiring is about the account's end date, a different question.

prompt: List the accounts that are locked out right now
why: LockedOut is worked out by the directory, so Get-ADUser -Filter cannot search on it. Search-ADAccount can.

prompt: List the domain users whose password never expires
why: Service accounts often have this set, which is why they are worth listing.

prompt: Show every group the user jsmith belongs to
why: This asks about one account's groups. Get-ADGroupMember asks the opposite: one group's members.

prompt: List the members of Domain Admins, including the members of groups nested inside it
why: Nested groups hide administrators. The switch is -Recursive; -Recurse belongs to Get-ChildItem.

prompt: Show the domain's default password policy
why: Length, age, history, complexity and lockout in one object: the first thing to compare with a baseline.

prompt: Show jsmith's last logon date and when the password was last set
why: Get-ADUser returns a short default set. Anything else has to be asked for with -Properties, or it comes back empty.
